We introduce Verifiable Agentic Biotechnology (VAB), a theoretical framework built on three provable guarantees. First, conformal prediction converts point estimates of biological fitness into finite-sample confidence intervals, guaranteeing coverage of true physical fitness with probability at least 1α irrespective of model misspecification. Third, the in-silico to in-vitro reproducibility gap is formalized as a Wasserstein distribution shift, yielding a Distributionally Robust Optimization bound V * DRBO on wet-lab transferability. Each bound is validated on controlled proxy environments and, in the case of conformal prediction, on real protein sequence data. While those frameworks address marketlevel coordination failures and employer-side information problems, Employment Latency specifically addresses the individual-level structural burden of repeated manual search effort across employment cycles, which persists even in efficient markets with low frictional unemployment and high information quality. The paper defines three measurable dimensions of Employment Latency: Discovery Latency, the time cost of manually monitoring fragmented opportunity sources at each search cycle; Application Latency, the effort cost of repeatedly generating tailored application materials from the same underlying profile information; and Verification Latency, the post-offer delay imposed by compliance verification processes that duplicate prior institutional verification of the same individual. The paper presents cross-sector evidence of Employment Latency in the UK labour market, analyses the technical architecture of an autonomous employment agent implementing the framework, and discusses policy, commercial, and research implications.
